title: Middle East conflict extension cuts global Q4 2026 crude run forecast by 1.4 million b/d
gist: Wood Mackenzie cuts its global Q4 2026 crude run forecast by 1.4 million b/d as the Middle East conflict extends and Ukrainian drone strikes take 3.5 million b/d of Russian refining capacity offline, but frames today's elevated Asian refining margins as temporary — Dated Brent is expected to fall to $50-60/bbl once Strait of Hormuz flows normalize, leaving only deeply chemical-integrated, energy-efficient refiners (increasingly Chinese) competitive by 2035.

insights.claim: Extending the Middle East conflict to year end cuts Wood Mackenzie's global crude run forecast by an estimated 1.4 million b/d in Q4 2026, with Asia bearing the brunt of the disruption.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A 1.4 million b/d cut to global refining throughput is a direct input to Q4 diesel and gasoline supply forecasts — a leading indicator for refined-product crack spreads into year-end.
insights.locator: opening paragraph, Extending the Middle East conflict to year end

insights.claim: Persistent Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries compounded the Middle East-driven disruption, taking unit outages to 3.5 million b/d in August and tightening the global refining system further.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Two independent supply shocks (Middle East conflict, Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries) are compounding simultaneously — a reminder that refined-product tightness has more than one geopolitical trigger to monitor concurrently.
insights.quote: unit outages at 3.5 million b/d in August, tightening the global refining system further
insights.locator: Persistent Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries

insights.claim: Alan Gelder describes the scale of disruption to global crude runs as being without modern precedent, while noting Asian refiners face an immediate margin opportunity but must decide how to respond strategically.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A WoodMac executive calling this disruption unprecedented is itself a signal worth weighting heavily when sizing refining-sector tail risk into Q4.
insights.quote: The scale of disruption to global crude runs is without modern precedent
insights.locator: quote from Alan Gelder, SVP refining, chemicals and oil markets research

themes.theme: Margins: elevated now, a $50/bbl world ahead

insights.claim: US and European refiners are deferring scheduled maintenance into 2027 in order to capture currently elevated refining margins driven by the Middle East and Russia/Ukraine conflicts.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Deferred maintenance concentrates turnaround risk into 2027, which could amplify any future supply disruption when that backlog of maintenance eventually has to happen.
insights.locator: Margins: elevated for now, a $50/bbl world ahead

insights.claim: Diesel markets remain strong due to Russian export constraints, continued inventory reductions and increased winter heating demand, while gasoline prices are likely to decline seasonally though limited Atlantic Basin supply should support margins through year-end.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Diesel cracks look structurally supported into winter while gasoline cracks face seasonal softness cushioned by Atlantic Basin supply limits — a product-level divergence worth trading distinctly rather than treating refining margins as one number.
insights.locator: Diesel markets remain strong due to Russian export constraints

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie forecasts Dated Brent will decline to the $50-60 per barrel range once Strait of Hormuz transits are fully restored, as non-OPEC production growth is set to exceed global demand growth in both 2027 and 2028.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: This is the key medium-term price call: current elevated margins and crude prices are a temporary conflict premium, not a new floor — investors should not underwrite refining or upstream projects on today's price levels persisting past a Hormuz resolution.
insights.locator: As non-OPEC production growth is set to exceed global demand growth in 2027 and 2028

insights.claim: Alan Gelder frames today's elevated margins as a down payment on transformation, warning that a lower oil-price environment combined with approaching peak oil demand will quickly expose the gap between competitive and uncompetitive refining assets.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Refiners and their investors banking today's windfall without reinvesting in competitiveness risk being caught uncompetitive once margins normalize downward — a capital-allocation signal for anyone holding refining equity or credit.
insights.quote: Refiners must treat today’s windfall as a down payment on transformation
insights.locator: quote from Alan Gelder following the Dated Brent forecast

themes.theme: Asian demand: scarred and slow to recover

insights.claim: Asia Pacific oil demand is not expected to return to pre-conflict levels until late 2027, following a projected 1.24 million b/d decline in 2026, with petrochemical feedstocks (especially LPG and naphtha) hit hardest while road fuels remained more resilient.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: An 18-month-plus demand recovery lag implies petrochemical feedstock demand (LPG, naphtha) stays structurally weak longer than headline oil demand numbers suggest — relevant for anyone pricing Asian petchem margins.
insights.locator: Demand: scarred and slow to recover

insights.claim: India is leading the regional demand recovery, surpassing pre-conflict demand levels first, with Southeast Asia following, while China's oil demand likely peaked before the conflict began.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A Wood Mackenzie call that China's oil demand has already peaked — independent of the current conflict — is a structural bearish signal for long-term Chinese crude import growth and reinforces India as the marginal demand-growth story in Asia.
insights.quote: China's oil demand likely peaked before the conflict began
insights.locator: India is leading the regional recovery

themes.theme: Crude sourcing shift and rising import dependency

insights.claim: Asia's crude import dependency is expected to reach 82%, with an additional 1.5 million b/d of imports by 2030, shifting the supply mix toward long-haul barrels from the US and Latin America as the Middle East's share of Asian crude imports declines from over 65% today.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Rising long-haul US/Latin American crude flows to Asia mean higher freight intensity and tanker demand, and a structurally lower Middle East share of Asian trade — a durable shift in crude trade routes for shipping and logistics investors to price in.
insights.locator: Crude supply: recovering, but Asia's import dependency rising to 82%

insights.claim: Sushant Gupta argues refiners that can optimise across a wider crude slate, particularly grades with higher middle-distillate yields, will be best positioned to capture value as Asia's crude supply base structurally diversifies.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Crude-slate flexibility becomes a competitive moat as sourcing diversifies — a screening criterion for identifying which Asian refiners will retain margin advantage through the transition.
insights.quote: The conflict has accelerated the structural diversification of Asia’s crude supply base
insights.locator: quote from Sushant Gupta, director, oils and refining research

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Refinery Evaluation Model identifies deep chemical integration as the primary margin driver for Asian refiners going forward, with second-generation integrated sites achieving chemical yields above 40% and much higher net cash margins than first-generation sites; partial integration is not sufficient for first-quartile competitiveness.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Screen refining assets by chemical-yield percentage, not just capacity — partial integration is explicitly flagged as inadequate for top-quartile returns, a concrete filter for refining-sector equity selection.
insights.quote: Second-generation integrated sites with chemical yields above 40% achieve much higher net cash margins than first-generation sites.
insights.locator: Refinery competitiveness: deep integration and energy efficiency are the decisive levers

insights.claim: By 2035, nearly 80% of top-performing refineries are expected to be Chinese assets with extensive chemical integration, implying most non-Chinese Asian refiners will fall behind on competitiveness absent similar integration investment.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: This is a strong concentration call — Chinese integrated refiners are expected to dominate the top competitiveness tier by 2035, a structural headwind for refining assets in Japan, Korea, and Southeast Asia that don't pursue comparable integration.

insights.claim: About 55% of refineries currently exceed the global benchmark for energy intensity, and the least competitive refineries also tend to have higher energy intensity, indicating substantial room for efficiency-driven margin improvement.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Energy-intensity benchmarking is a quick screening proxy for refining competitiveness — assets clustered above benchmark energy intensity are the likeliest candidates for closure or forced capex under the coming lower-margin environment.
insights.locator: Currently, about 55% of refineries exceed the global benchmark

insights.claim: Alan Gelder argues that for many refiners, import substitution and margin competitiveness are effectively the same investment decision, as global peers actively reshape portfolios ahead of the 2035 outlook.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Frames refining capex decisions as a single strategic choice rather than two separate ones — useful lens when evaluating capital-allocation announcements from Asian national oil companies and integrated refiners.
insights.quote: For many refiners, import substitution and margin competitiveness are the same investment decision.
